newsitem.title: USA: Conn. governor vows reductions of gas, income tax.
newsitem.headline: Conn. governor vows reductions of gas, income tax.

text.p: Connecticut Republican Gov. John Rowland vowed Wednesday reductions in the state's gasoline and income taxes, and promised to follow through on calls to remedy segregation in Hartford's schools.
Rowland outlined his broad proposals in his annual state of the state address at the opening of the 1997 legislative session on Wednesday.
Rowland, Connecticut's first Republican governor in 20 years, is expected give specifics when he presents his formal budget in early February.
"By the end of this session, I will commit to you and I hope that you will commit to me, that everyone's taxes will be lower," Rowland said to a round of applause in the chamber.
He also warned the state against wasteful spending.

"If we return to a pattern of introducing new programs every session, spending our surplus or raiding the rainy day fund, we know what the result will be -- more deficits, higher deficits and more taxes in the future," he said.

Rowland said that any tax cuts "must benefit as many people as possible. We all realize that the gas tax increases approved by the previous administration are nothing less than highway robbery, and we will make cuts in the gas tax during this session."
He also said the income tax "picks the pockets of the working people of this state."
While Rowland has long favored cutting the personal income tax, he faces a tough fight with state Democrats who would rather emphasize reductions in property taxes, political analysts said.
Democrats, who controlled the state's House of Representatives, gained control of the State Senate in the November elections.

Senate Democrats Tuesday offered an agenda that included increased spending for higher education and for student financial aid, and a slew of other initiatives on education, crime, health care, campaign finance and economic development.
Many Democrats favor a proposed property tax cut known as the circuit-breaker.
The circuit-breaker concept has been debated and rejected at the state Capitol in recent years.
"There is tangible anger in the state over property tax burdens," New Haven Mayor John DeStefano Jr said in a statement on Wednesday.
DeStefano attended the opening session of the General Assembly to lobby in favor of the circuit-breaker.

"Take the property tax in combination with the fact that Connecticut has experienced the longest and most severe economic slump since the Great Depression, and you have a major quality of life issue for the state," said DeStefano.
